13261:
There are several things you can do to check out all of the user replaceable parts if you have 1 working unit.
1) Swap power supplies. If the unit comes up then you have solved one     problem. Try this with both, using the same "good" supply.
2) Swap the RF modulators (the silver box located in front on the left     side like above. It would be advisable to leave the cord on.

3) Remove the RF shield. there are 5 different types so I cant tell you     exactly. If you feel more comfortable, just bend it up.
4) If you have a multimeter, and are comfortable using it, there are 4     necessary voltages that need to be close. If any are bad STOP.    a) +5 Volts appears all over the board, but it will be easier to     check 3 of them on the memory chips.
        You'll need to remove the keyboard plastic as described below    the data chip is like this   GND            +5V
    x x x x x x x x
    ----------------   |               |    )              |   |o              |   -----------------    x x x x x x x x
  -5V             +12V                  +15V
    +12V is newer, the original used +15V
    The +10V supply can be found on the Custom Address (middle one) pin     40 which id the one nearest the power supply connector, in the back     of the chip.    These are all referenced to ground. The entire chassis is ground.

5) CAREFULLY, with the power off, replace the Custom I/O chip. It's the     40 pin one nearest to the hand control port #1. To remove, place a     skinny screwdriver between the chip and the socket and lift     carefully. Once one side is clear of the socket, start removing the     other side. When placing in the socket be CAREFUL to get all 20 pins     on one side into the socket slightly, and then align the other 20     pins with the holes in the socket and push down. If it really doesn't     want to go in, there might a bent pin. It will need to be slowly     straightened and try again.
6) Repeat step 3 for the other 2 Custom chips. To replace the DATA chip,     you'll need to remove the keyboard / cartridge slot plastic by     removing the 4 screws on the bottom. Be careful here also. The      switches are connected to a PCB under the buttons. The wires are     somewhat fragile. 
    If you have any problem doing these, please give me a call @     1-937-247-5664. I will be out of the country Dec 8-16.
Ken Lill

13269:
For what it's worth, I consult for the primary company behind the most
popular TV games, AtGames, and I can tell you that something like an
Astrocade Flashback would never become a reality. Flashbacks are low cost,
mass market products, and they rely on volume for sales success. I won't go
into specifics, but I can say that anything outside of Atari and Sega stuff
to this point has not sold well, and we're talking platforms (which again,
I won't mention specifically) that were light years ahead of the Astrocade
in terms of popularity and game libraries. If modern "recreations" of those
well remembered products struggle to sell, an Astrocade Flashback wouldn't
stand a chance, which is why a company like an AtGames would never do one,
since we're talking sales targets not in the hundreds of units, but in the
hundreds of thousands of units for it to be viable.

In fact, it wouldn't even be part of their new digital strategy, which is
allowing them to expand their offerings to PC and mobile to include some of
the less popular second and third tier platforms. Although the Astrocade is
cool, to be fair, it's not even anywhere near a third tier platform (a good
barometer might be how many people out of a random group of say 25 people
would know what the heck you're talking about if you mention a
platform--you could probably push that number to 1000 and you still might
not get anyone who knows what an Astrocade is). The other issue of course
is having enough games to license and make available for play, and I
honestly don't even know the state of such things with the Astrocade. Even
some of the more popular platforms with libraries quadruple the size of the
Astrocade's can be a struggle to find a sufficient number of somewhat known
games to legally license.

At the same time, there are lots of other communities - for instance Atari
5200 and Turbo-Grafx/16 fans - who have been calling for the same thing,
and the answer is more or less the same (though sometimes for different
reasons): No/Not going to happen. While those platforms stand a chance as
digital offerings (which is far less risk and easier to pull off than
physical hardware), the point is, it's something that a lot of communities
(with far more enthusiasts than the Astrocade) want and think would sell,
but don't realize that a few hundred to a few thousand enthusiasts that
remember what is now an obscure platform don't make for a mass market
audience (and I'm not saying that's the case here - I know it's not, i.e.,
these were just off-hand wishes).

Now, to make my long-winded point... There is actually a potential way to
pull this off in spirit. The potential is that there are alternatives that
don't require big companies. These include FPGA recreations, emulators for
Android platforms (for play on things like the Nvidia Shield or Ouya, for
instance), etc. All of that is well within reach of the homebrew community
should sufficient desire/interest (and skill and time, of course) be there.
In fact, considerable progress has been made in both areas for a variety of
platforms. So, while wishing for something like an Astrocade Flashback is
pointless, wishing for an FPGA recreation or a good Android emulator could
actually lead to something we could buy. Especially with the FPGA, that
would create an alternative platform once more of our Astrocade consoles
start to bite the dust.

Anyway, just my two cents...

I don't understand the numbers on the unit with no power.  What is the G# ?If you are saying the +5 is 4.97xxx, That's perfect. It may have something open, though.All power supplies are critical, though.The +12V only goes to the RAM chips. On the one with the aluminized plastic top shield, that will probably be +15VThe +10V goes to all of the custom chips and modulator.The -5V goes to the RAM chips and modulator.in addition to these. The DATA chip generates +2.5V and ONLY goes to the modulator to give the LM1889 chip +10V referenced to the +2.5V, a +7.5 bias. The -5V is also referenced to the +2.5V, giving it a -7.5V.Thus the LM1889 sees a 15V biasing, riding on the +2.5V as the ground reference.Ken Lill

13281:
I hope your pins 1 are minus 5. If so, the black screen looks OK except I don't know what the +10V is on either.
If none on the no power, you probably have 1 or more bad diodes in the PS. OR C6 could be shorted, and last but not least, if the 10V is good, you probably have a shorted memory chip.

if the latter, snip pins 8&9 on one memory chip at a time. If one if the supplies comes up, you probably found the main culprit. Do not solder the others back until you replace the one you just found, then tack one back in at a time and check again. If you find more than one bad, you'd probably be better off replacing all of them.
If you just have 4164 RAMS, they will work but need modifcation to the supply pins.Ken

13287:
Hey Gang,

I found this group not too long ago and this is my first “post”.

First off, to the guys that have been talking about living in Ohio, I live in Cincinnati.

I have an Astrocade that I got years ago and dabbled quite a bit in both hardware and software modifications.  Nothing too elaborate, just a lot of experimenting.  I made a cartridge with an eprom socket so that I could write my own assembly / machine code programs and store them.  I wrote a few short, fun little programs just playing around, in both assembly language and BASIC.  I always wanted to get one of those hybrid systems like ZGrass, but stopped messing with it before I did.  I always loved the system and would enjoy messing around with it again, but not sure I have the time it would take to remember how to get it all going and how to use it again.  I think if someone could get me back up to speed quick enough, I would invest the time.

I was professionally programming in Z80 assembly language for imbedded systems at the time, so I had all the tools and knowledge to be decent at knowing the Astrocade from the inside.  I had eprom burners and lots of other electronics equipment at my disposal.  I also had a Z80 assembler and had written a Z80 disassembler, so I had poured thru a lot of the code seeing how things worked.  I had subscribed to Arcadian and had learned a lot through it.  I had forgotten a lot of this and had to consult the website just to remember the names like, ZGrass and Arcadian.

I am a Mac user (although I use and support PCs too) and saw that there is an emulator for the Astrocade.  I would be very interested in making that work.  I have downloaded MacMESS, but I guess I haven’t gotten all the other pieces needed, so I haven’t got it working yet.

Anyway, cool that interest for this system is still around.  I am still fond of it.

Thanks,
Marty

This is the reality where the Bally Home Library Computer was the number-one selling computer in the seventies and eighties.  This led to their current machine, Bally Z-GRASS Superkit 4.  This awesome machine sits at number one beside the second-place Odyssey Deluxe, Model 5 (with Build-In Voice Synthesizer) and the third-place Fairchild Power-Pack Color Module 6 (now with external controllers).  In that reality the families really DO smile like the parents and kids on the boxes of those old '70s game boxes!

As a reminder, I made a posting in 2006 (which was made into an article) about a sort-of Astrocade Flashback in 2006.  The article is called "Bally Arcade "Retro Astro" Handheld Unit by ToyMax!"  You can read it again, or for the first time, here:

I expected this to be the case.  The Bally barely sold this well the first time around over the course of seven years (reportedly it sold 300,000 units.  Does anyone know the original source of this oft-quoted number?).  I was actually very surprised (but delighted) to see that their was going to be a Colecovision Flashback.  As much as I like the system, it was barely a blip in the grand scheme of consoles.  Plus, it was soon eclipsed by the much better-selling Coleco Adam (just some sarcasm there, in case it doesn't come though clearly).

I wouldn't have bought the Colecovision Flashback (I've never owned any other Flashback), but when I found out that it came with my favorite Colecovision game, Antarctic Adventure, I went to the nearest Dollar General (the only place that sold it with that game-- which I found strange) and snatched one up.  I didn't even know that an Intellivision Flashback existed until I saw it at the same time of purcase.  I bought that one too as an impulse buy.  I actually like the Intellivision Flashback more.  Mostly because the Colecovision's sound is pretty far-off from the original.  I'm glad I own them though.  They both cost something like $84 with tax, which is significantly cheaper than, say, a nice dinner out with my wife.  Of course, the Flashbacks don't offer love in return... but you can't have it all, right?

About the sound being off with the Colecovision.  You'd probably only notice it if you owned a Coleco.  If you haven't played one since 1986 or, especially, if you've never used one at all, then you'd just think the system was designed that way.  It's a shame in a sense, but I'd much rather have a Colecovision Flashback that works pretty-good and allows new users to be introduced to this neat system than to have only collectors remember it as something they played (or wanted to play) when growing up.  I think it's great that my friend who lives in a town of 8,000 people here in New Mexico is the one who actually told me about it.  Not because he saw it online, but because he saw it in a store and just purchased it thinking it might be neat to try out.  That is what makes the Flashbacks so great-- availability to the masses.

For what it's worth, I consult for the primary company behind the most popular TV games, AtGames, and I can tell you that something like an Astrocade Flashback would never become a reality. Flashbacks are low cost, mass market products, and they rely on volume for sales success. I won't go into specifics, but I can say that anything outside of Atari and Sega stuff to this point has not sold well, and we're talking platforms (which again, I won't mention specifically) that were light years ahead of the Astrocade in terms of popularity and game libraries. If modern "recreations" of those well remembered products struggle to sell, an Astrocade Flashback wouldn't stand a chance, which is why a company like an AtGames would never do one, since we're talking sales targets not in the hundreds of units, but in the hundreds of thousands of units for it to be viable.
In fact, it wouldn't even be part of their new digital strategy, which is allowing them to expand their offerings to PC and mobile to include some of the less popular second and third tier platforms. Although the Astrocade is cool, to be fair, it's not even anywhere near a third tier platform (a good barometer might be how many people out of a random group of say 25 people would know what the heck you're talking about if you mention a platform--you could probably push that number to 1000 and you still might not get anyone who knows what an Astrocade is). The other issue of course is having enough games to license and make available for play, and I honestly don't even know the state of such things with the Astrocade. Even some of the more popular platforms with libraries quadruple the size of the Astrocade's can be a struggle to find a sufficient number of somewhat known games to legally license.
At the same time, there are lots of other communities - for instance Atari 5200 and Turbo-Grafx/16 fans - who have been calling for the same thing, and the answer is more or less the same (though sometimes for different reasons): No/Not going to happen. While those platforms stand a chance as digital offerings (which is far less risk and easier to pull off than physical hardware), the point is, it's something that a lot of communities (with far more enthusiasts than the Astrocade) want and think would sell, but don't realize that a few hundred to a few thousand enthusiasts that remember what is now an obscure platform don't make for a mass market audience (and I'm not saying that's the case here - I know it's not, i.e., these were just off-hand wishes).
Now, to make my long-winded point... There is actually a potential way to pull this off in spirit. The potential is that there are alternatives that don't require big companies. These include FPGA recreations, emulators for Android platforms (for play on things like the Nvidia Shield or Ouya, for instance), etc. All of that is well within reach of the homebrew community should sufficient desire/interest (and skill and time, of course) be there. In fact, considerable progress has been made in both areas for a variety of platforms. So, while wishing for something like an Astrocade Flashback is pointless, wishing for an FPGA recreation or a good Android emulator could actually lead to something we could buy. Especially with the FPGA, that would create an alternative platform once more of our Astrocade consoles start to bite the dust.
Anyway, just my two cents...===================================================

Bill Loguidice, Managing Director; Armchair Arcade, Inc.

13290:
Not to take this too far off the Astrocade topic, but there were an
unfortunate series of events that didn't allow the new Intellivision and
ColecoVision Flashbacks to be as good as they should have been, mostly
resulting from a miscommunication with the hardware engineers. For
instance, both were originally supposed to have backwards compatible
controllers. Each has one broken game. The colors and sound are fairly far
off on the ColecoVision Flashback, the joystick nub shaft is too short, and
the left/right buttons are reversed from their usual functions (I wrote the
game descriptions in the ColecoVision Flashback manual based on the idea
that the controllers would function like the originals and there would be
speech in Squish'em Sam). Etc. (There are also other reasons that I won't
get into why the Intellivision Flashback is better.)

The bottom line though with all of the above in mind, for a $40 mass market
product, compromises always have to be made. It's sometimes hard for fans
to appreciate that, just like many people will complain about "missing"
games (not appreciating that you just can't put any game on there - it
needs to be legally licensed). Hopefully most, if not all, of these issues
will be fixed for the sequels, assuming of course that sales justify
sequels (and that's not a given, obviously).

In any case, to bring this back to the Astrocade, I also agree that the
first order of business should be getting quality Astrocade emulators onto
the most popular platforms. I'd also like to know what the legal status is
of many of the games, which might allow for at least some of the titles to
be legally bundled with an emulator. The good news is that few were
licensed in any way, so that should make the ownership path and the
potential release of rights a little clearer.

-Bill

Quite a few Astrocade programs have been put into the public domain.  Most of these are all tapes, but a couple of them are carts.  There is a PD FAQ, which hasn't been updated since 2002.  You'd think the FAQ would be rather outdated... but it's actually not too far off.  Here it is:

Highlights in the list are all of George Moses Co., New Image and  Wavemakers tapes.  That's many dozens of programs.  Those programs are all among the best tape releases for the Astrocade.  However, there is no emulator that supports loading tapes, so unless you have the actual hardware, then it's not easy to play them.  Brett Bilbrey 's two carts (ICBM Attack and Treasure Cove) are PD.  That's great, because they're both quite good-- and very hard to find in cart format.  Those two carts work fine under the MESS Astrocade emulator.  There is an article about the cart PD releases here:

Not to take this too far off the Astrocade topic, but there were an unfortunate series of events that didn't allow the new Intellivision and ColecoVision Flashbacks to be as good as they should have been, mostly resulting from a miscommunication with the hardware engineers. For instance, both were originally supposed to have backwards compatible controllers. Each has one broken game. The colors and sound are fairly far off on the ColecoVision Flashback, the joystick nub shaft is too short, and the left/right buttons are reversed from their usual functions (I wrote the game descriptions in the ColecoVision Flashback manual based on the idea that the controllers would function like the originals and there would be speech in Squish'em Sam). Etc. (There are also other reasons that I won't get into why the Intellivision Flashback is better.)
The bottom line though with all of the above in mind, for a $40 mass market product, compromises always have to be made. It's sometimes hard for fans to appreciate that, just like many people will complain about "missing" games (not appreciating that you just can't put any game on there - it needs to be legally licensed). Hopefully most, if not all, of these issues will be fixed for the sequels, assuming of course that sales justify sequels (and that's not a given, obviously).
In any case, to bring this back to the Astrocade, I also agree that the first order of business should be getting quality Astrocade emulators onto the most popular platforms. I'd also like to know what the legal status is of many of the games, which might allow for at least some of the titles to be legally bundled with an emulator. The good news is that few were licensed in any way, so that should make the ownership path and the potential release of rights a little clearer.

As much as I like the system, it was barely a blip in the grand scheme of consoles.  Plus, it was soon eclipsed by the much better-selling Coleco Adam (just some sarcasm there, in case it doesn't come though clearly).

13300:
On the ColecoVision Flashback, "The Heist" runs at 50% of its normal speed,
more or less in slow motion. On the Intellivision Flashback, "Tower of
Doom" does not allow for melee attacks. As for the scrolling in
"Destructor," it was always choppy like that. Speaking of "Destructor,"
it's one of the games I featured in the ColecoVision chapter of one of my
recent books, "Vintage Game Consoles." It's definitely a love it or hate it
type of game. For me, it was always love it, and I think for its relative
unique nature and ambition for the era, even with its technical flaws (the
final release was a bit rushed), make it a worthwhile experience (note that
the original required the steering wheel; this is the modern day hack for
the standard controllers).

"Squish 'em Sam," was one of only three pre-Crash console cartridge games
that talked without the need for extra hardware. The other two were "Spike"
on the Vectrex and "Quadrun" on the Atari 2600. Of course, the first
cartridge-based games to feature digitized sound were on the Tandy Color
Computer (CoCo), with the 1980/1 releases of "Skiing" and "Dino Wars."

As for the Flashbacks on TVs, the display quality varies greatly between
CRT, Plasma, LCD, LED, etc. It sometimes appears there's no rhyme or
reason, with some being much sharper than others, some having the picture
cut off, etc. Ideally, these would all have HDMI output, but that's not
practical at the target price point (and it needs to be at that price,
otherwise the retailers wouldn't carry it).

I also agree about the Astrocade controller. Without a reasonable
fascimile, you not only lose out on functionality, but also a great deal of
the platform's charm.

Bill Loguidice wrote:
>>
I wonder why there were no other overlays made for the Astrocade other than [these six: ADS System Monitor, BASIC, General Video Assembler, Machine Language Manager, Music Maker and Scribbing?]?
>>

I expect that there were so few Astrocade overlays because they required more effort to manufacture.  The typical systems that have them (Intellivision and Colecovision) just have small pieces of plastic that slide over a chiclet keypad.  The Astrocade's overlays require 24 small rectangle-shaped holes be punched into each overlay for each button.  The effort required to create these overlays for third-party tapes companies wouldn't have generally been worth the effort.

The only high-quality third-party overlay is for "Machine Language Manager.  It looks as good as the one for Bally BASIC.  The overlay for General Video Assembler is pretty intricate for a third-party (it's made of plastic), but you can tell that the color was added by-hand with a marker.  That's time consuming.  Music Maker's laminated paper (not plastic) overlay uses a shortcut that requires only six extra-wide rectangles to be created.  The ADS System Monitor only has a plain paper overlay, and only one of these overlays may exist, as the cart was a prototype that's not even finished.

There is actually one additional overlay that I can think of that's not listed on the webpage that Bill pointed to with all the other overlays.  This missing overlay was for a program printed in the Arcadian.  I think it was a paint program that required extra RAM, and it may have even have required some other additional hardware.  Does anyone remember for which program that overlay was created?

>>
It seems like it would have been interesting to "enhance" at least a few of the games with some fun overlays.
>>

Yes, a few carts could have used it.  Even if just for fun-- and they weren't needed.  Certainly the prototype Coloring Book would have required one if it had been released.  That would have been released by Astroivision.  The prototype Color BASIC would have required one too, but that was a hack by an individual and wasn't meant to be sold.

I have to disagree with that statement, Lance.  I think Muncher is pretty rare, much more rare that "The Incredible Wizard."  Maybe it's that way in Canada?  Back in 90s, in the U.S., when finding Astrocades wasn't that hard (I found, at least, six systems this way-- most not working, of course), I think most of those systems actually came with "The Incredible Wizard."  I've also found it loose and boxed on several occasions in the wild.  While I do own "Test Programme," I've never found it in the wild.

MESS
 isn't user friendly at all, which is a shame.  It does work with most
cartridges and is your only emulator option.  Sometime back (a couple of years ago), it was upgraded and it sorta broke, so
now some carts no longer work and I think the timing is off a bit (maybe that's just me).  It doesn't support tapes I/O, but for
general game-playing it does an okay job.  The main problem most people
have with MESS is knowing where to put the Bally 8K ROM.  That ROM is
included in this pack (as are cart ROM images):

http://www.ballyalley.com/emulation/cart_images/ROMs/astrocade_rom_collection.zip

The
 on-board ROM (System ROM) goes into a directory under MESS called ROM.
 There are three ROMs, which all work pretty-much the same (you'll
probably not notice any difference yourself).  Cart images go into a
directory under MAME called software/astrocde.  If you do that, then
MESS should start without complaining.  I'm not sure if MacMESS requires
 more info, but I doubt it.  You'll still need to set up controllers and keypad (especially if you plan to give BASIC a while-- even just to type in a short "HELLO WORLD" program.  Pressing Tab will bring up a list of options that you can change.
There is a MESS user manual that should be able to guide you the rest of
 the way:

http://www.mess.org/mess/howto

>>
I think if someone could get me back up to speed quick enough, I would invest the time.
>>

What do you need to know?  I'll try to give you a general overview to get you going.

There are many Z80 cross-compilers (of course), but the best choice for the Astrocade is one called ZMac.  That's because you can use the header file that was used at Bally (Nutting Associates, actually) back in 1977.  It makes creating something fairly quick because there are many, many system calls to routines that are very helpful.  Here's a link to ZMac:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_tools/Zmac13_win32.zip

The manual with everything you're looking for is "The Handbook of Hardware & Software" (generally referred to as the "Nutting Manual," as Dave Nutting Associates is really the force behind the Bally Arcade).  That "Nutting Manual" is here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/nutting%20manual/nutting_manual_project_2-1.pdf

This version of the manual was retyped and can be searched.  Other specifically Astrocade machine language programming information is here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/ml_docs.html

Plenty of general Z80 reference material is available here (and all over the web, really):

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/z80_docs/z80_docs.html

There is some source code (mostly disassembled from the carts) to get you up and running to use as ML examples:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/ml_source.html

In general, everything you need to program the Astrocade is available in this area:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml.html

It would be great if there was a document that had all this sort of information in it already.

I hope that this helps get you up and running.

Adam

I worked out of a mom and pop computer store in the 90s called "University Computers."  They're long gone.  It was there that I saw SO many different configurations of the Amiga 2000 montherboard.  And the wildest Amiga in abouit 1996/97: a A4000 with a toaster and $25,000 worth of hard drives.  I contacted NewTec to get the machine fixed and they were leading me through the most elementary tasks.  All the while it was obvious that they were disassociating themselves with Commodore and the Amiga name.  I finally had to break it to the tech that I understood what was going on and that I was an Amiga tech.  After that the call went smoothly and the computer was fixed.

Some of the earliest Amigas that I saw had MB fixes (made by Commodore, I presume).  I saw many dead CIAs and leaked clocked batteries (in one case it destroyed the motherboard beyond repair because the computer stood on its side).  Those were some fun days-- it was always neat to interact with the Amiga community.

I also ran into some other strange computers.  I recall that one guy came in looking for new tapes for his Coleco Adam in 1998.  He still used the machine.  It was his ONLY computer.  He wasn't so much a die-hard either.  He was an old guy and that's what he could afford and its what he knew.  I miss the days of many different computers.  In other ways I'm glad that they're gone.

I sold an Atari 800 (or maybe 400) with Eastern Front: 1941 (a very popular cart) and a joystick to one guy for $50.  He came in the next day just to tell me he'd stayed up half the night playing that game.  I can't say that I ever ran into any Bally users there, but I did run into people using Atari ST and other computers that many people thought didn't make it out of the 80s.

Sorry, this is all way-off topic.  While Colecovision and Intellivision Flashbacks make sense to talk about, Amigas probably belong to some other forum.

Adam

> MESS isn't user friendly at all, which is a shame.  It does work with most cartridges and is your only emulator option.  Sometime back (a couple of years ago), it was upgraded and it sorta broke, so now some carts no longer work and I think the timing is off a bit (maybe that's just me).  It doesn't support tapes I/O, but for general game-playing it does an okay job.  The main problem most people have with MESS is knowing where to put the Bally 8K ROM.  That ROM is included in this pack (as are cart ROM images):
>
> http://www.ballyalley.com/emulation/cart_images/ROMs/astrocade_rom_collection.zip <http://www.ballyalley.com/emulation/cart_images/ROMs/astrocade_rom_collection.zip>
>
> The on-board ROM (System ROM) goes into a directory under MESS called ROM.  There are three ROMs, which all work pretty-much the same (you'll probably not notice any difference yourself).  Cart images go into a directory under MAME called software/astrocde.  If you do that, then MESS should start without complaining.  I'm not sure if MacMESS requires more info, but I doubt it.  You'll still need to set up controllers and keypad (especially if you plan to give BASIC a while-- even just to type in a short "HELLO WORLD" program.  Pressing Tab will bring up a list of options that you can change.  There is a MESS user manual that should be able to guide you the rest of the way:

> There are many Z80 cross-compilers (of course), but the best choice for the Astrocade is one called ZMac.  That's because you can use the header file that was used at Bally (Nutting Associates, actually) back in 1977.  It makes creating something fairly quick because there are many, many system calls to routines that are very helpful.  Here's a link to ZMac:
>
> http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_tools/Zmac13_win32.zip <http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_tools/Zmac13_win32.zip>
>
> The manual with everything you're looking for is "The Handbook of Hardware & Software" (generally referred to as the "Nutting Manual," as Dave Nutting Associates is really the force behind the Bally Arcade).  That "Nutting Manual" is here:
>
> http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/nutting%20manual/nutting_manual_project_2-1.pdf <http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/nutting%20manual/nutting_manual_project_2-1.pdf>
>

> http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/z80_docs/z80_docs.html <http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/z80_docs/z80_docs.html>
>
> There is some source code (mostly disassembled from the carts) to get you up and running to use as ML examples:
>
> http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/ml_source.html <http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/ml_source.html>

     Hey Gang,
I found this group not too long ago and this is my first “post”.
First off, to the guys that have been talking about living in Ohio, I live in Cincinnati.
I have an Astrocade that I got years ago and dabbled quite a bit in both hardware and software modifications.  Nothing too elaborate, just a lot of experimenting.  I made a cartridge with an eprom socket so that I could write my own assembly / machine code programs and store them.  I wrote a few short, fun little programs just playing around, in both assembly language and BASIC.  I always wanted to get one of those hybrid systems like ZGrass, but stopped messing with it before I did.  I always loved the system and would enjoy messing around with it again, but not sure I have the time it would take to remember how to get it all going and how to use it again.  I think if someone could get me back up to speed quick enough, I would invest the time.
I was professionally programming in Z80 assembly language for imbedded systems at the time, so I had all the tools and knowledge to be decent at knowing the Astrocade from the inside.  I had eprom burners and lots of other electronics equipment at my disposal.  I also had a Z80 assembler and had written a Z80 disassembler, so I had poured thru a lot of the code seeing how things worked.  I had subscribed to Arcadian and had learned a lot through it.  I had forgotten a lot of this and had to consult the website just to remember the names like, ZGrass and Arcadian.
I am a Mac user (although I use and support PCs too) and saw that there is an emulator for the Astrocade.  I would be very interested in making that work.  I have downloaded MacMESS, but I guess I haven’t gotten all the other pieces needed, so I haven’t got it working yet.
Anyway, cool that interest for this system is still around.  I am still fond of it.
Thanks,Marty

    For what it's worth, I consult for the primary company behind the most popular TV games, AtGames, and I can tell you that something like an Astrocade Flashback would never become a reality. Flashbacks are low cost, mass market products, and they rely on volume for sales success. I won't go into specifics, but I can say that anything outside of Atari and Sega stuff to this point has not sold well, and we're talking platforms (which again, I won't mention specifically) that were light years ahead of the Astrocade in terms of popularity and game libraries. If modern "recreations" of those well remembered products struggle to sell, an Astrocade Flashback wouldn't stand a chance, which is why a company like an AtGames would never do one, since we're talking sales targets not in the hundreds of units, but in the hundreds of thousands of units for it to be viable. 
In fact, it wouldn't even be part of their new digital strategy, which is allowing them to expand their offerings to PC and mobile to include some of the less popular second and third tier platforms. Although the Astrocade is cool, to be fair, it's not even anywhere near a third tier platform (a good barometer might be how many people out of a random group of say 25 people would know what the heck you're talking about if you mention a platform--you could probably push that number to 1000 and you still might not get anyone who knows what an Astrocade is). The other issue of course is having enough games to license and make available for play, and I honestly don't even know the state of such things with the Astrocade. Even some of the more popular platforms with libraries quadruple the size of the Astrocade's can be a struggle to find a sufficient number of somewhat known games to legally license.
At the same time, there are lots of other communities - for instance Atari 5200 and Turbo-Grafx/16 fans - who have been calling for the same thing, and the answer is more or less the same (though sometimes for different reasons): No/Not going to happen. While those platforms stand a chance as digital offerings (which is far less risk and easier to pull off than physical hardware), the point is, it's something that a lot of communities (with far more enthusiasts than the Astrocade) want and think would sell, but don't realize that a few hundred to a few thousand enthusiasts that remember what is now an obscure platform don't make for a mass market audience (and I'm not saying that's the case here - I know it's not, i.e., these were just off-hand wishes).
Now, to make my long-winded point... There is actually a potential way to pull this off in spirit. The potential is that there are alternatives that don't require big companies. These include FPGA recreations, emulators for Android platforms (for play on things like the Nvidia Shield or Ouya, for instance), etc. All of that is well within reach of the homebrew community should sufficient desire/interest (and skill and time, of course) be there. In fact, considerable progress has been made in both areas for a variety of platforms. So, while wishing for something like an Astrocade Flashback is pointless, wishing for an FPGA recreation or a good Android emulator could actually lead to something we could buy. Especially with the FPGA, that would create an alternative platform once more of our Astrocade consoles start to bite the dust.
Anyway, just my two cents...

    Bill Loguidice wrote:
>>
I wonder why there were no other overlays made for the Astrocade other than [these six: ADS System Monitor, BASIC, General Video Assembler, Machine Language Manager, Music Maker and Scribbing?]?
>>

I expect that there were so few Astrocade overlays because they required more effort to manufacture.  The typical systems that have them (Intellivision and Colecovision) just have small pieces of plastic that slide over a chiclet keypad.  The Astrocade's overlays require 24 small rectangle-shaped holes be punched into each overlay for each button.  The effort required to create these overlays for third-party tapes companies wouldn't have generally been worth the effort.

The only high-quality third-party overlay is for "Machine Language Manager.  It looks as good as the one for Bally BASIC.  The overlay for General Video Assembler is pretty intricate for a third-party (it's made of plastic), but you can tell that the color was added by-hand with a marker.  That's time consuming.  Music Maker's laminated paper (not plastic) overlay uses a shortcut that requires only six extra-wide rectangles to be created.  The ADS System Monitor only has a plain paper overlay, and only one of these overlays may exist, as the cart was a prototype that's not even finished.

There is actually one additional overlay that I can think of that's not listed on the webpage that Bill pointed to with all the other overlays.  This missing overlay was for a program printed in the Arcadian.  I think it was a paint program that required extra RAM, and it may have even have required some other additional hardware.  Does anyone remember for which program that overlay was created?

>>
It seems like it would have been interesting to "enhance" at least a few of the games with some fun overlays.
>>

Yes, a few carts could have used it.  Even if just for fun-- and they weren't needed.  Certainly the prototype Coloring Book would have required one if it had been released.  That would have been released by Astroivision.  The prototype Color BASIC would have required one too, but that was a hack by an individual and wasn't meant to be sold.

Adam

Bill Loguidice wrote:>>I wonder why there were no other overlays made for the Astrocade other than [these six: ADS System Monitor, BASIC, General Video Assembler, Machine Language Manager, Music Maker and Scribbing?]?>>I expect that there were so few Astrocade overlays because they required more effort to manufacture.  The typical systems that have them (Intellivision and Colecovision) just have small pieces of plastic that slide over a chiclet keypad.  The Astrocade's overlays require 24 small rectangle-shaped holes be punched into each overlay for each button.  The effort required to create these overlays for third-party tapes companies wouldn't have generally been worth the effort.The only high-quality third-party overlay is for "Machine Language Manager.  It looks as good as the one for Bally BASIC.  The overlay for General Video Assembler is pretty intricate for a third-party (it's made of plastic), but you can tell that the color was added by-hand with a marker.  That's time consuming.  Music Maker's laminated paper (not plastic) overlay uses a shortcut that requires only six extra-wide rectangles to be created.  The ADS System Monitor only has a plain paper overlay, and only one of these overlays may exist, as the cart was a prototype that's not even finished.There is actually one additional overlay that I can think of that's not listed on the webpage that Bill pointed to with all the other overlays.  This missing overlay was for a program printed in the Arcadian.  I think it was a paint program that required extra RAM, and it may have even have required some other additional hardware.  Does anyone remember for which program that overlay was created?>>It seems like it would have been interesting to "enhance" at least a few of the games with some fun overlays.>>Yes, a few carts could have used it.  Even if just for fun-- and they weren't needed.  Certainly the prototype Coloring Book would have required one if it had been released.  That would have been released by Astroivision.  The prototype Color BASIC would have required one too, but that was a hack by an individual and wasn't meant to be sold.Adam

I looked through the last volume of the Arcadian for the last overlay.  It's printed along-sie the "Light-Pen Graphics Program."  Here's the complete information about it:

Although the "Arcadian" doesn't state that any additional hardware or software is required to run the program, according to Mike White's "Tape Programs Listing and Database FAQ," this program requires Blue Ram BASIC, 16K and a light pen.  The BASIC program is rather long, but besides probably needing to build your own light pen (neither Bally nor Astrocade provided one), you also needed expanded RAM and an extended BASIC to run the program.  Once you typed the program in and got it working, you'd still have to contend with no documentation.  Ouch!

Bill Loguidice wrote:
>>
I wonder why there were no other overlays made for the Astrocade other than [these six: ADS System Monitor, BASIC, General Video Assembler, Machine Language Manager, Music Maker and Scribbing?]?
>>

I expect that there were so few Astrocade overlays because they required more effort to manufacture.  The typical systems that have them (Intellivision and Colecovision) just have small pieces of plastic that slide over a chiclet keypad.  The Astrocade's overlays require 24 small rectangle-shaped holes be punched into each overlay for each button.  The effort required to create these overlays for third-party tapes companies wouldn't have generally been worth the effort.

The only high-quality third-party overlay is for "Machine Language Manager.  It looks as good as the one for Bally BASIC.  The overlay for General Video Assembler is pretty intricate for a third-party (it's made of plastic), but you can tell that the color was added by-hand with a marker.  That's time consuming.  Music Maker's laminated paper (not plastic) overlay uses a shortcut that requires only six extra-wide rectangles to be created.  The ADS System Monitor only has a plain paper overlay, and only one of these overlays may exist, as the cart was a prototype that's not even finished.

There is actually one additional overlay that I can think of that's not listed on the webpage that Bill pointed to with all the other overlays.  This missing overlay was for a program printed in the Arcadian.  I think it was a paint program that required extra RAM, and it may have even have required some other additional hardware.  Does anyone remember for which program that overlay was created?

>>
It seems like it would have been interesting to "enhance" at least a few of the games with some fun overlays.
>>

Yes, a few carts could have used it.  Even if just for fun-- and they weren't needed.  Certainly the prototype Coloring Book would have required one if it had been released.  That would have been released by Astroivision.  The prototype Color BASIC would have required one too, but that was a hack by an individual and wasn't meant to be sold.

13337:
I have added the first 2000-BAUD program to BallyAlley since July 3, 2014.  This new addition to the website is called "Light-Pen Graphics Program" by Leroy Flamm.  This program requires Blue Ram BASIC, 16K and a light pen.  The original source of the program is: Flamm, Leroy G. "Light-Pen Graphics Program." Arcadian, 7.4 (Aug. 15, 1986): 68-69. Print.

The "Light Pen Graphics Program" can be downloaded here:

http://tinyurl.com/ohekyk6

(or use the full URL:)

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/programs_i-p/Light-Pen%20Graphics%20Program%20(1986)(Leroy%20Flamm)(2000%20baud)(Blue%20RAM%20BASIC)(PD).zip

The program consists of two different loads, although I'm not sure why.  Paul, could you shed some light on this?

Mr. Flamm created a light pen of his own, probably in about 1983 or 1984.  Information about the device can be found in a letter he wrote to Mike White in a document I've called "Light Pen Plans and Schematics."  You can view that here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/misc_hardware_docs/full_size/Lightpen_Plans_%28Leroy_Flamm%29.pdf

These plans show how to build a light pen for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade. The documentation refers to a tape with a program for the hardware.  I can't be certain, but that program is probably "Light-Pen Graphics Program."  These plans, if also sent to Bob Fabris, editor of the "Arcadian," were never published (nor have I seen them in the Fabris collection).  Without the Leroy's light pen, the program would have been quite difficult to use without contacting Leroy Flamm for additional information (luckily, his address was printed along with the program in the newsletter).  With the extra RAM and Blue Ram BASIC, plus the build-your-own hardware required, it is really a wonder that the program was printed at all.  Perhaps it found its way into the last issue of the Arcadian to use-up some of the remaining stock of unpublished programs that Bob Fabris had never published.

Now that the program, overlay and hardware plans are finally together, all that is missing is documentation for the program, which was also not printed in the newsletter.  It's possible that no instructions were created because, maybe, the overlay in the newsletter was enough to understand how the program worked.  The overlay (just added to the website earlier today) is here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/keypad_overlays/full_size/Light-Pen%20Program%20%281986%29%28Leroy%20Flamm%29.gif

I want to thank Bill Loguidice for getting me spurred to investigate into other keypad overlays available for the Astrocade-- even though he didn't request it directly.  Overlays are an area of the Bally Arcade that I've always thought was really a great.  It wasn't unique for the time, but it went well used, even if only because it allowed for Bally BASIC to be created, which otherwise would not have been released until a keyboard was released by Bally, which never occurred.

Thanks also to everyone else for keeping me interested in the Bally Arcade.  It's the recent flurry of activity that keeps me updating the site.  By that logic, one would presume that the more everyone chit-chats on the discussion group, the more the website will be updated on a regular basis.  If so, then keep on talking!

The Bally Arcade is one of my favorite systems too (if the BallyAlley website was enough of a hint for you).  I personally like finding information out about it more than I like playing it.  Also, the Z80 is hardly unique for U.S. game systems (the Colecovision used it too), but other than CP/M, not nearly as many systems used the Z80 as systems from overseas.  The Z80 is fun to play around with-- especially on the Astrocade since the on-board ROM has good documentation for the ROM routines used in many of the game cartridges.  The instruction set on the Z80 is much larger (and complicated) than the 6502's set.  This doesn't make it better, just, you know... different.
The Atari 8-bit computers are my favorite 8-bit game machines (and computers in general).  I still love the 16 and 32-bit Amigas (my personal favorite is the Amiga 3000), but I finally gave all of mine away because my PAL monitors kept dieing on me; I got tired of replacing them (or, in the old days, having them repaired).  Sure, there is plenty of NTSC software for non-PAL TVs and monitors, but any Amiga user will tell you the real games (and demos) are from Europe.

13344:
I have three out of three working Astrocades. One of them has a special
(homemade) notch for a socketed EPROM cartridge. It's not much use since
the multicart, but still kind of neat. Considering what's genuinely
available for the Astrocade, I consider my collection more or less complete
with quite a few original cartridges, both BASICs, and all of the recent
homebrews. I'd of course love something like a computer add-on, but I don't
know if I'll see one for sale in my lifetime.

I like the Astrocade, but would put it somewhere in the 3 or 4 range in
terms of my collection. But then my collection is a bit excessive, so
that's actually not a bad score all things considered.

I have yet to play a tape game, though it's on my list to do eventually. I
also want to experiment with some solutions that eliminate the traditional
tape and see how that goes.

I haven't had much need to dabble in Astrocade emulation. Any time I've
used in a screenshot in a book or article, for instance, it's always been
captured off the real deal.

As for the Amiga stuff, I've lived perfectly well in the NTSC world, though
obviously having a PAL option to switch to is nice as well (in fact, my
main Amiga 1200 is a loaded PAL model, complete with compact flash). Also,
as with most systems, you can simply adapt it for HDMI with a cable and
then a powered adapter. For European systems I usually go SCART to HDMI,
but there are lots of options to go from x to HDMI. It's not always quite
as nice as a native monitor, but it usually looks great in my experience.
In any case, I generally keep a supply of Commodore 1084 monitors on-hand,
since they're incredibly versatile and usually have no problem handling
whatever signal I throw at it. I also have a small 13" world CRT TV that
can handle any signals that a 1084 or modern LCD/LED can't for whatever
reason (it's particularly good for Australian systems). Enough off-topic,
though...

-Bill

Sometime3s it's easy, and sometimes ALL of the TTL chips need to be replaced. That is usually when there has been a lightning strike or the transformer shorts out.
Custome chips are rare and hence the cost is very high. Approx $100.00 each.
Repairing the unit is $75.00 + parts. ALL ics and be replaced and usually for a minimum of cost. The same thing fdor the other parts except the modulator and the power supply which are also rare.
To check the power supplies, you'll need a volt meter and a Phillips screwdriver. If you have any electrinics experience, I could walk you through the first few checks. After that you will need an oscilloscope.

Ken Lill

13363:
I added "The Jailer Problem" by Fred Rodney to BallyAlley.com.  This short AstroBASIC program was submitted to the "Arcadian," on May 1, 1983, but it is previously unpublished.

Fred Rodney writes in a letter to Bob Fabris, editor or the "Arcadian" newsletter: "This is a listing in AstroBASIC of the 'Jailer Problem' in the June 1983 issue of Popular Computing, page 211. The Astrocade takes 2.75 minutes to complete this problem. I figure that the Astrocade does about 485 computations. That equals about 187 computations per minute or 3 per seconds. Each computation takes 333 milliseconds."

The program, as Fred said, is based on "The Jailer Problem," a puzzle posed by "Popular Computing" in the June 1983 issue. Here's the magazine's description:


To recap from last month: an eccentric jailer makes a complicated amnesty offer to his 100 inmates. Every second, he reverses the status of certain cell doors from open to closed or vice versa. After one second, he switches cells whose numbers are multiples of 1 (all of them are opened). After two seconds, cells whose numbers are multiples of 2 (even-numbered cells) are switched. After three seconds, he switches cells whose numbers are multiples of 3, and so on. He repeats this process for 100 seconds. If a cell door is open after the last switch, the con in that cell goes free.

Now, as we asked last month, which inmates will benefit from this amnesty offer?

The key to the solution of the problem is the recognition that a cell is switched once for each number that divides evenly into the cell number. For example, cell number 6 will be switched at seconds 1 (open), 2 (closed), 3 (open), and 6 (closed)-- these are the divisors of 6. If a cell number has an even number of divisors, then that cell will be closed when all the switching is over. Only cells whose numbers have an odd number of divisors will be open after all is said and done.

The program in listing 1 [not included here] finds and lists all the cells that will be open after the 100-second switching process. Why not type it in and try it out before continuing?

Did you notice the rather striking pattern to the cells that are open? Next time I'll offer an elementary mathematical explanation of why we get such an elegant result.


You can download the type-in AstroBASIC "Jailer Problem" here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/Jailer%20Problem%20(Fred%20Rodney).zip

If you type it in and save it to a digitally archived WAV file, then I'll archive it on the website.

Fred Rodney was a late Bally Arcade user that didn't seem to enter the Astrocade scene until it was late in the game.  All of Fred's programs are pretty neat; I'm glad that they're being archived.  Why not take a look through the website and see what else he wrote?

Have fun!

The Artillery Duel cart prototypes currently on-line come from Ken Lill's tape collection, and many of Ken's tapes are originally from John Perkins himself. So, these could be from any stage of development, and since none of them are in a playable state, they're unlikely to be the ones mentioned in this letter.
The scan came from Adam's portion of the Bob Fabris collection, and was the only document from Perkins Engineering in its folder, so I'm not sure that we could match it up to a particular tape with certainty. I honestly don't see anything that seems to completely match. The letter describes a 300 baud side of the tape, but searching through my recordings from Bob Fabris's tapes, my Artillery Duel tapes are 2000 baud only (unless of course there's a tape that's not labeled).
The only tape that looks like it MIGHT match is a 2000 baud only tape labeled "Artillery Duel, RAM 6K Astro BASIC INPUT %(24576) ROM 2K". This didn't process the first time I tried it, but I was able to get it working this time. The resulting ROM is an exact match to the commercially released cart.
Paul

The Artillery Duel cart prototypes currently on-line come from Ken Lill's tape collection, and many of Ken's tapes are originally from John Perkins himself. So, these could be from any stage of development, and since none of them are in a playable state, they're unlikely to be the ones mentioned in this letter.
The scan came from Adam's portion of the Bob Fabris collection, and was the only document from Perkins Engineering in its folder, so I'm not sure that we could match it up to a particular tape with certainty. I honestly don't see anything that seems to completely match. The letter describes a 300 baud side of the tape, but searching through my recordings from Bob Fabris's tapes, my Artillery Duel tapes are 2000 baud only (unless of course there's a tape that's not labeled).
The only tape that looks like it MIGHT match is a 2000 baud only tape labeled "Artillery Duel, RAM 6K Astro BASIC INPUT %(24576) ROM 2K". This didn't process the first time I tried it, but I was able to get it working this time. The resulting ROM is an exact match to the commercially released cart.
Paul

13381:
I added preliminary instructions for new users of Blue Ram BASIC 1.1 to BallyAlley.com.  At the time this one-page document was made, there was as yet no comprehensive set of BRB instructions.  With only these instructions (which don't even include a list of the new BASIC commands) and no manual for BRB, it would have been very difficult to figure-out how to use the expanded BASIC.

http://www.ballyalley.com/perkins/perkins.html#16K-32KPrelimDocs

It's no wonder that early users had such trouble with BASIC.  In my eyes, there never was a proper Blue Ram BASIC 1.1 manual.  Certainly nothing along the lines of the AstroBASIC manual.

Have fun!

Adam
13382:
I added a second version of the "Blue Ram - BASIC Operating System 1.0" manual to BallyAlley.com.

The "Blue Ram - BASIC Operating System" (1.0) is a machine-code program which runs in the Blue Ram.  It is composed of a GOSUB linker and an advanced editor.  The GOSUB linker provides all of the linkages necessary to access BASIC subroutines resident in the Blue RAM.  These five pages of instructions are for version 1.0 of what was to become "Blue Ram BASIC 1.1."  The BRB 1.1 cartridge supersedes Blue Ram - BASIC Operating System 1.0.

http://www.ballyalley.com/perkins/perkins.html#BlueRAMOS1

Enjoy!

Adam
13383:
I updated BallyAlley.com by adding 1980's Blue Ram BSR Controller driver and software by Perkins Engineering.  Although the software has been digitally archived, there were some issues during the archiving process.  Thus, the RAW tape file is also included which makes the download much larger than is usually required.  For much more details about the archiving issues, see Paul's original information when he uploaded the file to the FTP site (included in the software download link, below).

The Blue Ram BSR controller is an ultrasonic interface between the Blue Ram and the BSR X-10 home controller system. This combination allows the user to control lamps, overhead lights, and appliances under direction from your Bally Arcade. Up to sixteen "devices" may be controlled and may be anywhere on the common power line.   

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/perkins_engineering/perkins_engineering.html#BlueRamBSR

The previously unarchived manual for this BSR device has also just been added to the website too.  The link for that manual can be found in the BSR software link (above).  I'll also be making a posting about that update soon.

I'd say "Enjoy!" or "Have fun!," but I don't think that there is even one example of this BSR hardware left anymore... or does someone have it?  Did anyone ever seeing it working back in the 1980s?

Adam

1) Blue Ram 16K Owner's Manual - Already online, sorta.  I THINK this may be a slightly altered version.  Either way, this will be a better scan without my screwing around with the original like I used to do when I first started the BallyAlley site

I think next I'll add some programs that Paul suggested before I finish this Perkins documentation area.

Back in the day, most printers were individually designed by each company. Most shared the ASCII base set of characters, but all of the control characters were at the whim of the designer. Most dot matrix printers (25 pin Parallel port only) would work just fine if all you did was print out text. but when it came to print out special characters like extra wide, bold, italics and pictures, you were at the mercy of the manufacturer.Ken

     On Tuesday, February 17, 2015 3:59 PM, "Adam Trionfo ballyalley@hotmail.com [ballyalley]" <ballyalley@yahoogroups.com> wrote:



     I updated BallyAlley.com by adding 1980's Blue Ram BSR Controller driver and software by Perkins Engineering.  Although the software has been digitally archived, there were some issues during the archiving process.  Thus, the RAW tape file is also included which makes the download much larger than is usually required.  For much more details about the archiving issues, see Paul's original information when he uploaded the file to the FTP site (included in the software download link, below).

The Blue Ram BSR controller is an ultrasonic interface between the Blue Ram and the BSR X-10 home controller system. This combination allows the user to control lamps, overhead lights, and appliances under direction from your Bally Arcade. Up to sixteen "devices" may be controlled and may be anywhere on the common power line.   

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/perkins_engineering/perkins_engineering.html#BlueRamBSR

The previously unarchived manual for this BSR device has also just been added to the website too.  The link for that manual can be found in the BSR software link (above).  I'll also be making a posting about that update soon.

I'd say "Enjoy!" or "Have fun!," but I don't think that there is even one example of this BSR hardware left anymore... or does someone have it?  Did anyone ever seeing it working back in the 1980s?

Adam

 Subject: [ballyalley] Comments on Perkins Manual Not yet Uploaded

    I'm making some progress through the Perkins Engineering manuals, but it's slow-going.  I still have these eight left to go:

1) Blue Ram 16K Owner's Manual - Already online, sorta.  I THINK this may be a slightly altered version.  Either way, this will be a better scan without my screwing around with the original like I used to do when I first started the BallyAlley site

2) Blue Ram Assembly 4K Unit Instructions - Similar to above.  I think a similar version is online.

3) Blue Ram Diagnostic - The two-page manual is already online, but this is the program listing and it will complement it well-- uh, if it's for the right version!  Maybe I should combine the two documents.  What do you think?

4) Blue Ram Keyboard Manual - Already online (in much cleaner format without most mark-ups).  However, I think that this also may be a slightly different version.  Lots of little changes were going on.  I wonder how John and Clyde had time for Perkins Engineering with John working 40-hours a week for various companies.  This was a side gig.  I guess it was because Clyde was retired and could take care of many day-to-day activities.

5) Blue Ram Operations - This is eight pages.  The online version is only six pages.

6) Blue Ram Super-Extended BASIC 1.0 - There are two versions online already, and I think that this is also different.

7) Blue Ram Utility - Various versions of the Utility instructions are already online.  I'm not sure where this fits into the complicated Utility timeline.

8) Blue Ram Utility 2.3 - With this version added to the website (and the above version) there will be five slightly different versions of the manual online.  This one is for a previously undocumented version... I think!

Going through the versions take a lot more time than I remembered.  No wonder I stopped when I did!  It gives me a headache... but is neat in some strange way that I can't quite grasp.

I think next I'll add some programs that Paul suggested before I finish this Perkins documentation area.

Adam

13394:
I added more information and documentation about the "Blue Ram Utility."  Specifically I added the following:

1) "Blue Ram Utility 1.0" (?) - Information and Listing.  Contains a June 6, 1980 BASIC program listing, one-page of additions to the Blue Ram Utility documentation, and BASIC and Machine Code segments of the Blue Ram tutorial used in Arcadian, 2.9 (Oct. 7, 1982): 77-79.

2) "Blue Ram Utility 2.3" - Letter to Bob Fabris from Clyde Perkins dated June 1983, and Blue Ram Instructions.

I also updated the general description (as well as the description of each piece of documentation related to the utility).  I did this because the old descriptions were vague (or non-existent) and left people with no idea of what the utility could do, or how useful it is for machine language programmers.  This is the description that I added:

The "Blue Ram Utility," first released in 1980, is a powerful environment for Z80 machine-code programming on a Bally Arcade/Astrocade with a Blue Ram expansion and extra RAM. The utility was improved with each release over the next couple of years. By 1983, the "Blue Ram Utility 3.0" included a full-featured (full-screen) hex editor that utilized a small font, use of a modem, use of an EPROM burner, a disassembler, and the ability to test RAM in the Blue Ram as if it were a cartridge. Other related capabilities made this the best way to program in Z80 machine language on the Bally Arcade!

Though the utility was only officially released on cassette tape, version 3.0 eventually did find its way onto cartridge via homebrew methods in the mid-1980s.

All this information is here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/perkins/perkins.html#UtilityDocs

Have fun!

Adam

13397:
I know I've said this before, but I still find it amazing that a company
with such limited resources and little market presence would be able to
score not only a Conan license, but also a G.I. Joe license.

G.I. Joe Cobra Strike came out from Parker Brothers for the Atari 2600 in
1983, and Conan: The Hall of Volta came out from Datasoft for various
computer platforms in 1984, so it's clear those licenses were up for grabs,
but even assuming magazine lead times, for Astrovision/Astrocade to score
those licenses in 1982 is incredible, especially considering how
competitive the market was at the time for licensed stuff. Needless to say,
it's a story I'd LOVE to hear the REAL details on.

I do know that certain licenses were granted by medium, which is why
different companies could put out the same game depending upon if it came
out on cartridge, tape, or disk, or whether it came out on console or
computer. Perhaps there was something like that here? Nevertheless, I'm
still baffled.

-Bill

13402:
This was SUPER early in terms of using licensed IP for video games. Remember, Conan could have been the first home video game ever to spin off from a movie or comic book:
http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/press/Conan_%5BPress_Release_06-06-1982%5D.pdf
The first such game to come out ended up being Raiders Of The Lost Ark for the Atari 2600, I believe, in 1982. There was an earlier Tron game for the Intellivision, but I guess it wasn't directly based on a movie. It's kind of strange that this took that long to catch on. It just seems like an obvious idea to me.

http://www.polygon.com/2014/6/2/5762218/movie-based-games-e-t-atari
Paul

    Bill Loguidice wrote:
>>
I still find it amazing that a company with such limited resources and little market presence would be able to score not only a Conan license, but also a G.I. Joe license.
>>

Agreed.  Sometimes I do wonder how many of these old news items are true.  How much would a license have cost Astrocade, Inc. in 1982?  Was this before all the videogame companies were clamoring for licenses?  When exactly did the Conan movie come out on this timeline?

>>
I do know that certain licenses were granted by medium
>>

A good example of this is the Supercharger version of "Frogger" and the Parker Bros. version of the same game for the Atari 2600.  One on cassette tape and the other on cart.  I don't know of any Conan game on cartridge from that time period (or any time-frame, actually).  Datamost did make a Conan game, but it was only released on disk, I think.  Also (this is a long shot), could Astrocade, Inc. have used the name "Videocade" (an alternate name used by Bally for the carts) to loosen and open companies into a happier attitude to accept money for a license?  I'm thinking, "Nah, we don't make cartridges for the Astrocade.  We make Videocades, which are completely different."  I'm treading on thin ice with these ideas, I know!

Adam

I know I've said this before, but I still find it amazing that a company with such limited resources and little market presence would be able to score not only a Conan license, but also a G.I. Joe license. 
G.I. Joe Cobra Strike came out from Parker Brothers for the Atari 2600 in 1983, and Conan: The Hall of Volta came out from Datasoft for various computer platforms in 1984, so it's clear those licenses were up for grabs, but even assuming magazine lead times, for Astrovision/Astrocade to score those licenses in 1982 is incredible, especially considering how competitive the market was at the time for licensed stuff. Needless to say, it's a story I'd LOVE to hear the REAL details on.
I do know that certain licenses were granted by medium, which is why different companies could put out the same game depending upon if it came out on cartridge, tape, or disk, or whether it came out on console or computer. Perhaps there was something like that here? Nevertheless, I'm still baffled.

13407:
I guess I'll go with Esoterica's Star Trek (aka Starship Command). It's one of several simulation type space games for the system. Type in the coordinates you want to go to, randomly encounter enemies, use a menu to battle, that sort of thing. But really, I don't remember any of the Star Trek games being better than OK.
I suppose it's better than the first officially licensed Star Trek game, Star Trek: Phaser Strike for the Milton Bradley Microvision. Connecting to yet another recent topic, that's an extremely early example of a licensed video game, coming out in 1979.
http://en.memory-alpha.org/wiki/Star_Trek:_Phaser_Strike

Paul

13409:
I added two versions of a Perkins Engineering 4K Blue Ram schematic (9-30-1980) to BallyAlley.com.  First, there is the original scan from 1980.  Second, there is a new schematic made by Ken Lill in February 2015.

This schematic of the 4K Blue Ram is from the Bob Fabris collection. Its size is 21 3/4" x 16 1/2". That was too large to scan on my flatbed scanner. In order to archive the document, first I took a picture of the whole schematic. The quality of the picture is far too low to read because the image was taken with my camera (at its highest resolution: 180dpi jpg). The picture was taken from about six feet away. This picture is in color and was the only way that I could get a complete picture of the schematic at full-size. To get a readable final document, I scanned the schematic in four sections and then carefully stitched the pages back together by hand-- which took some effort but was worth it as the final TIFF is quite readable; you'll find it useful.

There is also a schematic of the 4K Blue Ram recreated by Ken Lill. He re-created the schematic using "OrCAD" (a schematic capture application by Cadence Design Systems) in February 2015. It took him about 6-8 hours to finish. Ken made some modifications to the original schematic: he kept the electrical exactly the same as it was before, but he did make some physical changes so that it would flow better. It now also fits on a B-Size sheet of paper (11" x 17") not D-Size (22" x 34"). Two pdf versions of the modified schematic are available in the zip archive: a full B size and a letter-size PDF for ease of printing.

This like will show you all of the various versions:

http://www.ballyalley.com/perkins/perkins.html#4KBlueRamSchematics

Have fun!

Adam
13410:
Seems like in the press release they forgot about the Atari 2600's Superman
game (1979) for one, and Spider-Man (1982 from Parker Brothers) for
another. It's also true that Mattel was the first to really go whole hog
with the licensing, getting sports and gaming associations for their
earliest games (late 70s), then later on expanding to licensing everything
else (early 80s), including movie (all TRON games WERE based on the movie,
FYI) and cartoon properties (like Hannah-Barbera). In any case, it would
have been very cool if Astrocade had actually released licensed product,
because outside of Atari, Mattel, and Coleco, I can't recall top of my head
any other pre-Crash companies licensing such products for their consoles.
Hopefully no money actually changed hands on the Astrocade side considering
they could have used those ultimately unused resources to help push their
ailing console.

I added an 8-page version of the "Blue Ram Operations Manual" to BallyAlley.com.  This document gives a general overview of what the Blue Ram upgrade can do and how to use it.  You can read it here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/perkins/perkins.html#BlueRamOperations

Specifically the manual provides details on the two on-board 8-bit bidirectional I/O ports (including pin diagrams), explains how the switch settings on the unit can set the Blue Ram's RAM to be ROM and then be used as a cartridge. It also includes a section on extended strings, and the Blue Ram Utility (including some of its intrinsic routines).

This replaces an alternate (probably older) version of the manual online which is missing information on extended strings and the "Blue Ram Utility."

Have fun!

Adam
13415:
I added two alternate versions of the "Blue Ram Super Extended BASIC 1.0" manual to BallyAlleycom.

This manual seems to be preliminary-- but it is all there really ever was: a regular manual was never created.  This covers the cassette version of "Blue
Ram Super Extended BASIC" (later to become "Blue Ram BASIC 1.1").  This
tape shipped with some versions of the Blue Ram expansion unit.  I think that this manual can be used with the BRB 1.1 cartridge.

You can read the manuals and examine the differences here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/perkins/perkins.html#SuperExtendedBASIC

These two alternate versions of the manual each have additional changes from one another; none of the three versions now online are identical.

1) Blue Ram Super-Extended BASIC 1.0 (19xx)(Perkins Engineering)(a1) - This alternate version of the "Extended BASIC" manual has a slightly different layout. Some of the information is presented in a different way.

2) Blue Ram Super-Extended BASIC 1.0 (19xx)(Perkins Engineering)(a2) - Seven pages. There are some hand-written notes, which seem to be corrections to the manual and some additional command examples.

It's pretty neat that so many different versions of Perkins Engineering manuals are now available on the website, but it's also pretty confusing.  Still, I'd rather have all the different versions of the manual, especially of these VERY rare items, than not have any of them at all.

Enjoy!

Adam

13421:
Pirate's Chase! - A Must Play Game!

Richard Degler mentioned recently on the Bally Alley Yahoo group message board that he had started to disassemble the code from the game, "Pirate's Chase!"  This is an Astrocade game that I had previously found quite dull, so I couldn't understand why Richard had decided to disassemble the game.  The technical aspect of the disassembly process (and assembly code) is always intriguing and of interest to me.  Richard basically said that it's not until you play the game with two players that it shines.  I've had it on my must-play list since then.  This week I finally did play a two-player game (several, actually)-- and I must say that Richard is right.  Way beyond right!  A two-player game of Pirate's Chase! changes it from a rather sedate Collect-the-Dots, almost passive way to kill some time, into a cutthroat battle for every treasure on the screen.  So, give "Pirate's Chase" a second look, you won't regret it, matey!

Here are some links related to "Pirate's Chase!" to get you ready to go!

1) This is the game being played by one person.  It looks, and is, plain looking-- and the gameplay won't attract your attention.  This is all so deceiving when a second controller is picked up by a foe-- I mean friend (but not for long!).

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w7PSTzYrbb4

2) Here's the manual (I've always particularly liked the cover art on this one):

http://www.ballyalley.com/cart_manuals/pdf_manuals/Pirates%27s_Chase_%28instructions%29%28astrocade%29%28color%29%28300%20dpi%29.pdf

3) This is a review of "Pirate's Chase" from the November 1982 issue of "Electronic Games:"

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/reviews/Pirates%20Chase/Pirate%27s%20Chase%20%28Electronic%20Games%29%28Review%29%28Nov%201982%29.pdf

4) Here is the Astrocade Top-Ten List "Article" (where "Pirate's Chase" sits on two people's lists):

http://www.ballyalley.com/ballyalley/articles/Top_Ten_Astrocade_Games.txt

5) The "Official Astrocade Scoreboard " from the October 31, 1984 issue of "Arcadian" lists Peggy Gladden's "Pirate's Chase!" score as 705,284.  Now that's an achievement!

http://www.ballyalley.com/ballyalley/articles/Official%20Astrocade%20Scoreboard.txt

Dig your Astrocade out at your next gathering and set up a two-player game of "Pirate's Chase!"  A quiet room will soon turn into a hollering party!

Adam
