I added 1982's "3D Tic Tac Toe" by General Video to BallyAlley.com.

This tape was found in Ken Lill's collection, not on the actual "Tape 821" as it was originally released.  This game includes a graphic title screen.

Here is some brief game background from a Tape 821 ad (see link provided
below for more details): "3-D board for greater challenge.  Joystick moves on each level,
 knob changes levels, trigger makes move.  Two human players or
challenge the computer!  Computer checks and displays winning row."

You can download "3D Tic Tac Toe" here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/steve_walters/steve_walters.html#3DTicTacToe

Here is an ad for Tape 821 from the SOURCEBOOK (Summer 1982):

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/steve_walters/3D_Tic-Tac-Toe/Tape%20821%20(1982)(General%20Video)%5BAd%5D.txt

I've always liked the "3D Tic-Tac-Toe" game for any system.  Usually the computer player is programmed pretty well.  I prefer the Atari 8-bit version or even the creaky Atari 2600 game.  I dare someone to have one of those systems play against the Bally.  You'd better use emulation, and you'd better use Warp Speed or else you'll be in for quite some wait.

Have fun!

Adam
13423:
I added 1982's "The Paper Chase"by Anderson Research and Design (A.R.D.) to Ballyalley.com.  This was programmed by Craig J. Anderson.

Paul Thacker comments, "This tape is from Ken Lill's collection, but not on official tape.  It includes a graphic title screen.  Turn the knob to aim and pull the trigger to grab toilet paper roll marked with black dot.  You have to grab it before the woman does, because she never misses.  The difficulty changes how quickly she grabs them.

"The Paper Chase is a funny idea.  Pretty simple game, but decent.  It is in 300 baud format already, but the 2000 baud version has more complete graphics.  The 300-BAUD version plays fine, but the graphics on the character on the right look incomplete compared to the 2000 baud version.  It's unclear whether or not this [2000-BAUD version was] released."

This program was originally on A.R.D.'s Tape G2, which also contained: Tic-Tac-Tollah, The Paper Chase, Micro-Pac, Caterpillar and Galactic Hitchhiker.

Here is some information from an ad from the SOURCEBOOK by RMH Enterprises, Summer 1982. Pages C10 and G13:

The Paper Chase: TV games should reflect TV reality.  Can Mr. Whipple snatch away the rolls of Toilet paper before the treacherous woman shopper squeezes him out of business?  It makes a better game than it does a commercial.

You can download the AstroBASIC version of "The Paper Chase" here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/hard/hard.html#PaperChase

This game is based on the "Don't squeeze the Charmin" TV commercials that ran from the 1960s into the 1980s.  An example of one of the commercials is here:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L50tuag6iRs

I haven't played this game yet, but it sure sounds strange, doesn't it?  I love these weird 70s and 80s anything-goes games!  If there was some weird idea that you had, and you had BASIC (and who didn't have it if they had a computer at that time?), then someone was programming it and trying it out.

Enjoy!

Adam

I think you misunderstood my comment. I didn't mean I wasn't sure if the 2000 baud version was released. It was advertised for sale, so I assume it was. I was talking about the graphics differences between the 300 baud and 2000 baud versions I archived. The 300 baud graphics look incomplete. I'm not sure if the 300 baud version was actually sold this way, or if I simply have an unfinished version. The archived 300 baud version comes from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. While I never had those physical tapes, I don't see it in the scans, so I assume it didn't come from a commercially released tape. The code might or might not be identical to what was actually sold.
The 2000 baud version is also not from a commercial tape (coming from Ken Lill's collection), but does look complete, with graphics matching the ads and review description, and a nice looking title screen.
Archiving this stuff gets complicated, doesn't it?

Paul

The built-in games are actually pretty good in that regard. Checkmate is the classic snake game for up to four players. I've definitely had fun with that one.
Gunfight is also multiplayer (just two in this case). I found it kind of repetitive after awhile, but it does make good use of the controller--move your character with the joystick, aim with the knob, and fire with the trigger.
Tornado Baseball / Tennis / Hockey / Handball have some interesting Pong variations.

But I really don't think you can beat The Incredible Wizard. I played the arcade version (Wizard Of Wor) at the Louisville Arcade Expo. It has more detailed monster sprites and voice samples, but it also gets hard really fast!

13462:
I added the first three issues of "Arcadians" to Ballyalley.com.  This is a round-robin letter that proceeded the "Arcadian" newsletter in 1978.

Look these over; they're short and you'll enjoy them.  These issues are a
 glimpse of the just flickering beginnings of the Bally Arcade, when
JS&A was still selling them only via mail-order, before BASIC was
released, and when people were having all sorts of issues with systems
not working and didn't yet know that to be a Bally Arcade owner means to
 be the proud owner of a quite fragile system.  Some of the early kinks
were worked out with the system failures, but as time has proven, the
failures have driven up the prices of working (and non-working!) units to this day.

Here's what you'll find in each issue:

1) "Arcadians" #1 - ARCADIANS, no. 1 (April 12, 1978): 1-2.

This first issue of "Arcadians" is simply referred to as "BALLY OWNERS."

This is the first letter to those who responded to an ad that Bob Fabris placed in "On-Line." This "issue" appears five months before the first "Arcadian" shipped in November 1978, starting off a seven-volume run (1978-1986).

Some of Bob's comments from the letter include: "Some game cartridges (cassettes, whatever - they have no tape in them) are available now [...]" I guess that calling the carts "cassettes" never settled right with anyone. Bob continues, "The Dial-A-Bargain add-on [basically, a modem to call JS&A] will be free to those who bought the unit before February 28, 1978." The Dial-A-Bargain never shipped. Bob also gives background about himself and his plans for the "group" (the people that got issue #1).

You can download it here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadians_vol_0.html#ArcadiansNo1


2) "Arcadians" #2 - ARCADIANS, no. 2 (May 29, 1978): 1.

You can download it here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadians_vol_0.html#ArcadiansNo2


3) "Arcadians" #3 - ARCADIANS, no. 3 (June 23, 1978): 1.


This is the first issue that is addressed to the "Arcadians."  I've always been fond of that nick-name.



This issues talks about someone who is a member of the "Arcadians" group
 went to the CES in Chicago and saw Tiny BASIC in operation.  Bally
BASIC is nearing completion; Bob has seen a copy of the BASIC manual.
He says that there are one-word summary of some BASIC commands. The game
 cart PCB is described as a 24 pin board with an IC on it that can't be
changed (a hand-drawn rendition of a Bally Arcade cartridge IC board is
included to give the reader a better idea of the description).

You can download it here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadians_vol_0.html#ArcadiansNo3

I'm really pleased with this new "Arcadians" download area.  I wish I'd taken the time to create thumbnails of the covers and had listed the general content of the other seven volumes of the "Arcadian" newsletters (and Cursor too).  Then again, the "Arcadian" newsletters were the first additions to BallyAlley.com (the reason it was created, in fact).  Back in 2001 I didn't understand how to setup a website.  As is plain to see from just how beautiful the website is now, I still don't know how to do it properly.  Ah, well, I'm happy it's available to all you classic gamers out there!

Have fun looking through these issues, which are the stone-age period of Bally citizenship.

Adam
13463:
I have added the final two issues of "Arcadians" before it was changed from a free round-robin newsletter to one that cost ten dollars a year.

Here is a description of each newsletter:

"Arcadians" #4
(ARCADIANS, no. 4 (September 1, 1978): 1-2.)

This is the first letter to those who responded to an ad Bob placed in "Kilobaud" magazine. There are about thirty-five people in the "Arcadians" group. Bob got his unit on February 28, 1978. A basic overview of hardware is given for new members of the group. Another mention of the overheating problem says that it only occurs with the first units that were shipped. NCE will send interested people a free copy of the TBASIC manual [printed on newspaper stock].

The Bally units in the Montgomery Ward's catalog increased in price from $220 to $269. Bob and about a dozen others (including Jay Fenton) have a meeting with Bally; they get to talk about what they want in the machine (and they also complain about problems that they've had). In the meeting Jay Fenton reviews a working prototype add-on unit (a rack-mounted 44K unit with a keyboard on a separate shelf. It includes a floppy disk system that broke on the way to the meeting).

The first mention of the "ZGRAS" programming language occurs in this issue. Eventually many users pin their hopes on this language and the add-under, both of which went unreleased-- at least for the Bally Arcade; the UV-1 computer, which included these functions (and more), did get released). ZGRASS has online help, which Jay demonstrates. Bob now has the code about the Bally Arcade routines available. Maybe he referring to the Nutting Manual? Information about the 50-pin connector is now also available from Bob.

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadians_vol_0.html#ArcadiansNo4


"Arcadians" #5
(ARCADIANS, no. 5 (October 10, 1978): 1-4.)

Bob exclaims in large hand-written letters, "It's Here!" He is referring to Tiny BASIC finally being on store shelves for $50. All members of the group are getting the Bally PA-1 Service Manual sent to them by Bally for free. Bob had been paying for postage and copying costs for all group members, so this is the last free issue. A one-year subscription costs $5 (the price increases to $10 soon afterward).

Bally says that a third vendor of the custom chips (address system, I/O and data) is now available to them. The Add-On will be demonstrated at the January 1979 CES show in Las Vegas. Bob mentions an article in the Sept/Oct issue of "Creative Computing" magazine. Bally is producing three different models of the unit. They are:

1) "BA-1000-2" - This unit is for Montgomery Ward.

2) "PBA-1100" - This model is available at retail outlets. Over 10,000 units of this model were manufactured at this point.

3) "PBA-1200" - This is the model available from the mail-order company JS&A.

Tiny BASIC and the cassette interface are discussed. The "Bally BASIC" errata sheet is included on page 2. Some commands that are not mentioned in the Bally BASIC manual are listed here. Eventually a document compiled by Jay Fenton called "Bally BASIC Hacker's Guide" includes all of these BASIC commands and how to use them). The cassette interface is said to be "somewhat touchy" and needs to be adjusted using the volume on the tape recorder. There is a reprint of the Tiny BASIC description from the Newman Computer Exchange (NCE) catalog (also reprinted on pages 7 and 8 of the premiere issue of "Arcadian").

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadians_vol_0.html#ArcadiansNo5

Thanks to Paul for spurring me to get these online... and reminding me that they were scanned and available; I'd completely forgotten about them.

Have fun!

13464:
I have added two completely different "Arcadians" subscription request letters.  These actually make MUCH more interesting reading than you'd imagine that they would.

Until now, the "Arcadians" have
been the hidden pre-history of the "Arcadian" newsletter.  What might
have happened if Bob Fabris, the editor, had not initiated the ball
rolling and started the "Arcadian?"  Would someone else have done it?
Maybe, although I'm really not sure if it would have been as good as the "Arcadian."  Bob was
quite devoted to getting the news out there in the beginning.  From his
records, it's amazing how hard he worked to get it done.

If someone
else HAD started a newsletter without the "Arcadian" existing first, then would it have lasted for seven volumes?  I can answer that for you.
No.  For example, just look at "The "Cursor" (later renamed BASIC Express), which was a Bally Arcade newsletter that started later, but folded
after three volumes.  Bob handed over editorship of his "Arcadian" to someone else for volume 7.  When the issues started falling behind, Bob came back to
wrap-up the last volume to give the "Arcadian" a graceful exit.  If the Bally Arcade/Astrocade had not had Bob, then even the few of us who know of the system now may never have heard of it.  That's impressive work!


"Arcadians" Subscription Request #1
(1978)

This is version one of the subscription request for the upcoming newsletter "Arcadians." This version says that the subscription amount is five dollars. This request may have been included with people that received "Arcadians" and/or sent to people who requested information about the upcoming newsletter.

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadians_vol_0.html#ArcadiansSubRequest1


"Arcadians" Subscription Request #2
(1978)

This is version two of the subscription request for the upcoming newsletter "Arcadians." The description of this request is completely different from the first one; it's not just reworded or a variant. The subscription amount has already increased from five to ten dollars. As with this first request, this one may have been included with people that already received "Arcadians" and/or sent to people who requested information about the upcoming newsletter. Eventually, when the first issue of the newsletter was released in November 1978, it had been renamed to "Arcadian."

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadians_vol_0.html#ArcadiansSubRequest2

I added fourteen prototype versions of "Frustration Fortress" by Ken Lill to BallyAlley.  This AstroBASIC game was published in the "Arcadian" newsletter in 1984 (see ARCADIAN 6, no. 8 (Jun. 30, 1984): 72).

Paul Thacker went through all fourteen versions and commented about each one (see the archive for details).  I never would have taken the time to archive all of these different versions, let alone also to keep a record of the details and differences between each one.  Thanks, Paul-- you're archiving skills are certainly to be reckoned with, aren't they?!?

Ken, do you have any comments about this game?

You can download all of the versions of the game here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/frustration_fortress_%5Bken_lil%5D.zip

I took the time to OCR the short instructions for this game from the Arcadian scan already online.  Since the print was so small it required plenty of fixes; I probably just should have re-typed it.

How to Play:

This is a one player game.  The object is to get all of the keys in each room without getting hit by any of the randomly firing Laser Cannons.  To move, use JX,Y(1).  TR & KN have no effect.  To get a key, all you have to do is touch it with the Blinking Box (your piece).

Scoring:

One point times the Round number is given for each key.  If you successfully finish getting the keys in a room, you must then go out the nearest doorway.  Make sure that you are completely within the door when you try to get out.  If you're not, you must reenter the room, line yourself up, and try again.  If you lose your man trying to get out (0 keys left) you will have to do the entire room again!  Otherwise if you lose a man, you will go back to the point that you left the last rack.

Extra Men:

You are awarded two extra men for completing the third round, and each four after that.  You get five men each time you get 500 points.


If playing with MANY different versions of a program is your thing, then this archive will certainly fit the bill.  Enjoy!

Adam

13475:
I added Ken Lill's 1984 "Blue Ram BASIC Operating Guide" to BallyAlley.com.  Paul Thacker went through a LOT of work to get this archived properly; thanks Paul, you rock!

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/programs_a-h/Blue%20RAM%20Operating%20Guide%20(Ken%20Lill).zip

The Blue Ram Operating Guide starts out explaining the operation of the Blue Ram hardware--how to connect it, what the switches do, etc.  This includes some images and animations.  The later sections are mostly text explaining the new commands in Blue Ram BASIC.

The final version of the "Blue Ram Operating Guide" requires 16K and is done in three loads (actually, each load is three separate loads).  When the load is done, it tells the user to turn off the tape (i.e. stop playing the archived file).  It also tells the user when to the "tape back on again.  Then the program automatically senses when the new load is started.  It then asks the user to wait for the load and then goes through its explanation again.

It took Ken Lill over three months to compile the tape that shows almost all of the features of the Blue Ram BASIC 1.1 in "real time."  It actually shows on the screen what the feature does, rather than the user needing to go through the manual (which can often leave the user wondering exactly what the commands do and how to use them).

There is no easy method to load the "Blue Ram Operating Guide" using AstroBASIC onto other Astrocade RAM expansion units like the Viper or Little White Ram.  An explanation of how it can be done is given (below), but it's not for those disinclined to experiment-- and probably run into failure a few times.  Originally these additional loading steps were not required; the program was meant to load via the Blue Ram's built-in 2000-Baud connection.


"How to Archive a Blue RAM Program" or
"Blue Ram Archival Notes"
By Paul Thacker
Dec 11, 2011

This text is referencing:

Blue RAM Operating Guide (1984)(Ken Lill).zip

This archive contains:

Blue RAM Operating Guide (Part 1) [...](Load 1 of 3).wav
Blue RAM Operating Guide (Part 1) [...](Load 2 of 3).wav
Blue RAM Operating Guide (Part 1) [...](Load 3 of 3).wav
Blue RAM Operating Guide (Part 2) [...](Load 1 of 3).wav
Blue RAM Operating Guide (Part 2) [...](Load 2 of 3).wav
Blue RAM Operating Guide (Part 2) [...](Load 3 of 3).wav
Blue RAM Operating Guide (Part 3) [...](Load 1 of 3).wav
Blue RAM Operating Guide (Part 3) [...](Load 2 of 3).wav
Blue RAM Operating Guide (Part 3) [...](Load 3 of 3).wav
Blue RAM Operating Guide (Part 4) [...](Load 1 of 4).wav
Blue RAM Operating Guide (Part 4) [...](Load 2 of 4).wav
Blue RAM Operating Guide (Part 4) [...](Load 3 of 4).wav
Blue RAM Operating Guide (Part 4) [...](Load 4 of 4).wav


While it obviously didn't follow as quickly from my meeting with Ken as I'd hoped, I am happy to say that I finally did get Ken's complete Blue RAM Operating Guide archived. There are a number of complications to doing this with the tools we have now, so it's worth detailing exactly what I did to make it happen.

While some Blue RAM programs just have a single load similar to what you'd see in Astrocade BASIC, the more complicated programs have three loads. The first one has a line to set up where the rest of the data gets loaded, and may contain some data to load into the regular system RAM. The second load is the main code of the program, and is loaded into the RAM expansion. The third load is very short, and sets up some variables.

These loads are sometimes spaced very closely together, which in and of itself can confuse ballybin. Additionally, some of the loads need to be treated differently, as I discovered. Therefore, I used Audacity to break the recording up into three different files. The trickiest one here is the second, which may be much larger than ballybin is used to dealing with. Only the Windows version of ballybin is capable of handling enough data. And this isn't standard BASIC code, so the BASIC load count should be set to zero. The first load is easier to process - in fact the earlier versions can do it as well. But keep in mind that this is treated like BASIC code, so if you use the Windows version, set the BASIC load count to one. This actually had me really confused for a while, because I couldn't figure out why I couldn't reproduce what I'd done with the first part of the guide program on the later parts. The third load, while shorter, is again not BASIC, so BASIC load count should be set to zero.

Doing it this way does mean that I ended up with three separate audio files. I just made a playlist of the files and started it up. Adam was kind enough to loan me his Blue RAM, which made testing much easier. Ken did send me some instructions for loading it into VIPERsoft BASIC. I had trouble following these because I started having problems consistently doing a warm reset. I believe they should work, however. I'm going to go ahead and upload the program to the group. If anyone tries this, please let me know:

1) Install Vipersoft (call 24576)

2) Type in GET %(!6000);GET %(!8FFC);GET
%(!6C20);%(!6C82)=!BF8B;%(!6FFC)=!9000;%(!6FFE)=!C072;BC=128

3) Load the tape using AstroBASIC, as we did for the 2nd part, but this time load all 3 [loads]

4) Now, hold the RESET button down and insert BRB 1.1, using the "Warm-boot" method.

There's a lot of information in the Operating Guide, and some cool animations and the first part, so I hope some people will get the chance to see it.

Now that I've gotten this going, hopefully I can knock out some additional programs from Mike White's compilation tape, which at this point is probably the densest source of unarchived Astrocade programs on the planet. After that, I should be able to fill in some gaps from Ken's collection and the Bob Fabris collection. I've also got some additional material that I worked on while the Blue RANDOM stuff was puzzling me.

Paul


Alternate versions of the program include:

1) Blue RAM Operating Guide 1.1 (1985)(Ken Lill)(2000 baud)(Blue RAM BASIC).zip - found in Ken Lill's tape collection on tape with type-written label.  In pen is written "MASTER COPY AS OF 11-19-85".  This includes a brief introductory part not found in version 1.0.

2) Blue RAM Operating Guide 1.1 (Part 2) (198x)(Ken Lill)(2000 baud)(Blue RAM BASIC)(proto)(Load 2 of 3).zip,
Blue RAM Operating Guide 1.1 (Part 2) (198x)(Ken Lill)(2000 baud)(Blue RAM BASIC)(proto)[a](Load 2 of 3).zip - found in Ken Lill's tape collection on tape with type-written label that says "BLUE RAM INSTRUCTIONS 1.1".  It only includes one load from this large program, however.  The tape also had two incomplete versions of Spring Thing, plus the program Tickets on the back.

3) Blue RAM Operating Guide (1984)(Ken Lill)(2000 baud)(Blue RAM BASIC)(proto)[a2].zip - found in Ken Lill's tape collection on tape hand-labeled "Blue RAM Instructions (1.0) Parts 1-3".  While the third part has a prompt to load the fourth part, it isn't on the tape.  The checksums are different than the version we got from Mike White, but otherwise I haven't checked for differences.

4) Blue RAM Operating Guide (Part 1) (198x)(Ken Lill)(Blue RAM BASIC)(2000
baud)(proto).zip,
Blue RAM Operating Guide (Part 1) (198x)(Ken Lill)(Blue RAM BASIC)(2000
baud)(proto)[a].zip - found in Ken Lill's collection on a tape hand-labeled
"Bball" that include a variety of programs in addition to the Tornado Baseball
ROM.


Well, enjoy the archive-- it has been a long time coming to the website!

Adam

I added George Moses "Astro Zap" to BallyAlley.com.  This version of the game has been modified for Blue Ram BASIC.  I'm not sure of what changes have been made to it.  Surely, at least, it has more colors.  Paul, can you give some details about this expanded version?

You can download the game here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/programs_a-h/Astro%20Zap%20(George%20Moses)(BRB).zip

I've added the "Astro Zap" instructions for the first time.  I was surprised that they're not online (in text form) already at BallyAlley, since this is one of my favorite AstroBASIC games.  These short docs were OCRed from the original Arcadian printing:


"Astro
 Zap" is similar to the commercial arcade game "Space Zap" by Midway,
only you don't need a quarter to play.  It will keep score for up to
four humans, using 1 hand control for each.  When you RUN the program,
input the number of players from the keypad.  When the game starts you
will use only the joystick to fire back at the invading missiles.  No
trigger is necessary.  You will receive 250 points for each missile you
eliminate.  A kamikaze will orbit your space fortress at random
intervals.  You must shoot it down before the second orbit or it will
dive into you.  Each human begins with three bases and will be awarded a
 bonus base every 10,000 points.  As points accumulate the missiles will
 travel faster until you can no longer keep up with the onslaught.  If
the missile hits the base there will be a terrible explosion which goes
on and on and on.  If you get sick of watching yourself explode, pull
the trigger to abort the fireworks.  This will bring up the next
player's turn.  The only other use of the trigger is at the GAME OVER
display if you wish to start a new game.


The original AstroBASIC printing of "Astro Zap" is called "Astro Zap 2000."  It was the $100 prize winner in July 1982 issue of Arcadian.  It's located in two Arcadian issues here:

ARCADIAN 4, no. 9 (Jul. 06, 1982): 88.   [Original Listing]
ARCADIAN 6, no. 10 (Aug. 24, 1984): 89.  [Reprint]

The original AstroBASIC game instructions and game listing can be viewed in the newsletter here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_4/arcadian_vol_4_issue_09.pdf#Page=4


There is a two-page ad for programs by George Moses in the Summer 1982 Sourcebook on pages G-14 - G-15.  Here is the short excerpt about "Astro Zap:"

"Astro-Zap!!!
 - Player-up sirens, fast action graphics, big explosions, bonus base,
Up to 4 players with up to 4 hand controls.  Kamikazes!  A real blast!!!
 Indicate Bally BASIC or AstroBASIC.  Free with purchase [...]"

A link to the first page of the "Sourcebook ad is here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ads_and_catalogs/sourcebooks/Sourcebook_1982_Summer.pdf#Page=64

Thanks for archiving this, Paul.  Also, thanks to Paul for making another Top 10 listing of programs that he wants to see added to the BallyAlley website.  This knocks off one of them.

Have fun, all you expansion RAM owners out there!  (I know that you've all been waiting with bated breath for expansion RAM games, right?!?)

Adam

I added a May 29, 1979 letter to Bob Fabris from Richard Belton.  Richard talks about the difficult time that he has reaching Bally, contacting Bob Weber, his own 48K RAM expansion (!), and more interesting information gleaned from the current Bally Arcade gossip from early 1979.

The Bob Fabris Collection is full of unique letters that are similar to these usually lost pieces of history.  You
certainly won't find unusual memorabilia like this on any other website
besides BallyAlley... until it's copied and then posted someplace else.  You can read Richard's letter here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/letters/letters.html#RichardBeltonLetter5-29-1979

Paul, do you care to point out anything else mentioned in the letter?

In Richard's letter he mentions a newsletter.  He is referring to "Arcadian Local News" May 30, 1979.  This 4-page hand-written newsletter was written by Richard Belton and published by/for the Maryland Users Group. Among other topics, Richard discusses a phone call that he made to Bally Corp. asking about the memory add-on and keyboard expansion. Bally sent a letter to Richard, which he included in the newsletter.  The newsletter is here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/misc_newsletters/Maryland%20Users%20Group%20Newsletter%20(5-30-1979).pdf

Have fun!

Adam

Drilling the holes in the hand controller for later access to the pots is a great idea idea!  I have a small box with about 12-15 Bally hand controllers.  All of them have something wrong with them.  Usually it's it's just pots-- but a few have cracked handles because someone (not me) got a bit too excited and enthusiastic while playing a game.  I've opened-up a few of these controllers before and cleaned the potentiometers using either contact cleaner or TV Tuner spray.  The pots eventually do get dirty again, but while they're working they are a dream to use.



I see that RadioShack still sells what is required to clean the controller's pots.  You can purchase "Control/Contact Cleaner and Lubricant" (Model: 6400148) for about $6 (plus shipping).  Here's a handy link to what you'd need:

http://www.radioshack.com/radioshack-control-contact-cleaner-and-lubricant/6400148.html#.VRAgzOG2Q8I

If you're pots are jerky when you move the knob around, then this will take care of the problem.  Be careful not to use too much of the spray!  It comes out fast, and you really only need a very small amount.

Adam

I added "Bots And Shots" by Bruce Brigden to BallyAlley.com.  This game for Blue RAM BASIC.  You can download the program here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#BotsAndShots

"Bots and Shots" is a modification of "Bots II" by Steve Walters.  "Bots II," in turn, is a re-worked version of "Bots" by Ron McCoy (first printed in the "Arcadian" newsletter, but later included on the "Best of Arcadian: 1980" tape).  The program listing and instructions for these two games can be found here:

McCoy, Ron. "Bots." ARCADIAN 2, no. 10 (Sep. 17, 1980): 90-91.

www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_2/arcadian_vol_02_issue_10.pdf#4

and here:

Walters, Steve. "Bots II." ARCADIAN 6, no. 7 (May 25, 1984): 61-62.

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_6/arcadian_vol_6_issue_07.pdf#1


Specific instruction for "Bots and Shots" are not available.  Here are instruction for "Bots II"
from the "Arcadian:"


"Bots II" is a reworked game originally submitted by Ron McCoy. The 9x19 playing field is sprinkled with walls (I) and Bots(*). Each time you pull the trigger, the Bots all move toward you. If they hit each other or a wall, they disappear

Bots II operates from Hand Control #1:

Knob - Controls the pointer as in the original version, for 8 possible directions of movement, or staying where you are if the pointer is not visible (far right or left turn of the knob). A sound was added for audible feedback when the pointer is moved.

Trigger - Fires the raygun if shots are left (shown at the bottom of the screen) and a Bot is within one square. Since it has a Bot sensor built in, it cannot be accidentally fired when they are out of range. The raygun sound effect is fun as the Bot vaporizes right before your eyes!


Joystick (forward or backward) - Moves you one square in the direction of the pointer, or ends your turn if you want to stay where you are.

As in the original version, after you move one square (or stay put), all Bots move one square toward you. If they hit a wall or another Bot, they are destroyed. If they reach you, you're dead! It still gets hairy once your raygun is out of power!


Have fun!

Adam

"Caterpillar"
(Revised)

By
Thadd*Pro (Kevin O'Neill), revised by Klaus Doerge

1986

Original
Versions: NIAGARA B.U.G. BULLETIN, 1.7 (September 6, 1983): 8-10.

These
directions are from the 1986 revision in the Arcadian newsletter.



Caterpillar
is a solo game of skill and luck, originated by Kevin O'Neill, published in the
ARCADIAN on August 24, 1984 in volume 6, #10, page 95, and now greatly enhanced
for virtually limitless play with scoring precisely tailored to the player's
performance.



The
Astrocade's accumulation limit of 32,767 has been bypassed and this rather addicting
game could easily become one of those we Arcadians will play competitively for
highest score.  The score limit on this
game is 32,789,999.



Caterpillar
progresses through 9 levels, within each, a floppy disk has to be moved 5 times
by touching it in order to reach the next, more difficult level. Sometimes the
caterpillar will go straight through the disk without further consequence and
you must return to it to touch it again before the disk is actually moved,
whereby the gap the removed disk leaves behind in the caterpillar's trail will
help recover smoothly from this tight looping. One must not penetrate any walls
or the caterpillar's trail or it will promptly disintegrate with rare
exceptions you cannot count on, however, constituting a glimpse of hope in case
of an emergency. If you must, you can make it through a wall, but it'll cost 1
or 2 blow-ups depending on the wall's thickness. - Don't worry, though; this
creature has 3 lives, thus giving you 3 chances on each level to make it through.
The time within which one has to complete each disk move is limited and a
timing bar under the score display, with a special warning after 75% of elapsed
time, enables you to monitor your status continually, because running out of
time is fatal to the caterpillar and final for the game. - One special word
about level 9 being, of course, the most difficult:

After
you have moved the disk 3 times and had no blow-ups, one barrier is eliminated
and an additional opening created so you can triumphantly finish this
ridiculously designed level.



Upon
completion of the 9th level you will be credited with 1000 bonus points, increasing
by 500 every time you do within the same game, after which the game will return
to level 1 by pressing TR, retaining your achieved score.



The
score is calculated as follows:



50
points for each disk move

x
the number of disks moved

x
the number of level you're on

-
the time used (total available time equals 160 points)

x
the number of blow-ups x 2

x
the number of level you're on



It
might happen that your first, or several early, scores on level 1 will produce
a negative number, but do not be discouraged - it'll progress into high numbers
quickly as you go on. Keep in mind, however, that running into walls or the
caterpillar's trail has an increasingly heavy toll on your score accumulation
and may, in fact, reduce your score at any given stage of the game. Also, time
limitation dictates to reach the disk via the shortest way possible,
remembering, however, not to create inaccessible areas with your caterpillar's
trail which often necessitates a quick decision on from what direction to best
approach that persistent disk.



An
average score after 9 levels without major disasters lies between 15,000 and 25,000.



Typical
score display:



2.6   1
16754 + 25K   2



(#
of level / fraction in increments of 2 tens toward the next level / # of set

of
9 levels you're on / Score / 25,000 points already reached / # of blow-ups

happened
on this level)



Be
meticulous inputting this program since there's only 15 bytes outside the listing
for execution.



Good
luck and much fun!!!

13497:
Room generation now working!

Long story,

When I started with the scroll demo, I was originally thinking of having a set number of rooms stored on cart, or generating it from reading code...

It made sense to me to build the room by walls rather than by spaces/sub rooms as there were less of them and I could use bit patterns to control them.

However, a good enough way to make proper rooms escaped me.

I briefly talked with a guy who had made a BerZerk clone for the C64. He was using a Maze generation routine that divided the Room/maze into smaller spaces/Sub rooms and checked if you could get to a room from an adjoining room.

It seemed like a big and cumbersome solution, but a workable one. However, I remembered seeing rooms with a box in the middle. So I asked about that and he admitted he had to fudge the routine to get that type of room to show up.

So, I let it sit there. Occasionally looking for a better solution.

Then I found this:

http://www.robotron2084guidebook.com/home/games/berzerk/mazegenerator/code/

I was stunned! I was closer worrying about the walls rather than the spaces, but it never occurred to me to even look at the pillars of the walls!

The actual arcade basically spins a single wall around each of the 8 pillars that line the middle of the room. This easily gives ample pathways and only occasionally do enough walls position themselves to make a box in the middle of the room.

I'm not entirely sure my routine is working exactly right, but it looks good. If it is close enough, it should make approx 870 odd mazes.

The resulting code I think is actually smaller that I was going to have with my old routine.

Anyway,

For your enjoyment, This version will continuously make rooms and scroll them off screen. It works great in MESS. I haven't tried it on an actual Bally/Astrocade yet. I worry it might overheat the video chip with all that scrolling...

Lance
